newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Filmmaker Loach remains angry crusader.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Filmmaker Loach remains angry crusader.

text.p: No one could accuse British film director Ken Loach of making populist feel-good films.

In his latest political epic, "Carla's Song", a Glasgow bus driver, a Nicaraguan dancer, and a former CIA agent are thrown into the turmoil of civil war in 1980s Nicaragua as fighting rages between Contra-rebels and revolutionary Sandinistas.

Loach, who was in Vienna to promote the film at the 1996 Viennale Film Festival, says the aim of his latest work is to throw light on alleged atrocities committed by the U.S.-funded Contras against the local community in Nicaragua.
"The Contra war was largely a hidden war because the Americans were the bad guys, so obviously America and its allies didn't want it spoken about too much," he told Reuters in an interview.
A smallish, self-effacing figure with a soft voice, Loach is an ardent champion of the working classes in the Hollywood-dominated filmworld.
Following in the European tradition of political realist cinema, he has a reputation for making audiences uncomfortable through the relentless honesty of his films.
"If you have the knowledge about something, then whether you want to or not, you have some responsibility and you can't escape that," said Loach.

In "Carla's Song" a Glasgow bus driver falls in love with a traumatised Nicaraguan dancer and freedom fighter. The two travel to her home, braving Contra raids, to find her lover, who has been disfigured in a guerrilla attack.
Loach, known for his strong leftwing views and socially critical films, presents a frank and brutal depiction of the war, making no bones about where his sympathies lie.
Loach's films are harsh, but not without a dark vein of humour.

"Riff-Raff" (1991) was about construction labourers exploited by unscrupulous employers in the early 1990s at the end of Margaret Thatcher's tenuire as prime minister. "Ladybird Ladybird" (1994), dealt with a single mother on the poverty-line. Both were a vivid picture of British working class lives.

"Raining Stones" (1993) is perhaps the least bleak to date, as a compassionate look at a Catholic father struggling to provide for his family, but determined to buy his daughter a costly communion dress.
"Land and Freedom", made in 1995, about the Spanish Civil war, was his first film tackling global politics.

Loach tends to work with a mixture of professional and virtually unknown actors, using minimum lighting and an improvised script to achieve as much spontaneity as possible. "The aim is to enable the actors to be who they are," he notes.

The most rewarding part of filming "Carla's Song", he says, was being able to give ordinary Nicaraguans a platform to speak. A scene on top of a bus where locals get carried away with whisky and tears as they discuss the country's political woes and forget the cameras is typical of Loach's style.

"The camposinos (peasants) in Nicaragua are the poorest, the most exploited and treated with contempt by the U.S. so to say "we want to hear what you have to say, we respect you', that was very important," said Loach.

Forthcoming projects are a documentary on the last dockers in the British port of Liverpool, who were made redundant last year, and two feature films set in Glasgow and the northern English city of Manchester.

Loach rejects criticism that his films are merely vehicles for his political views. "Films are terribly boring if they are just about the message. The characters exist in a social context and those are political stories."
He doubts he could make a Hollywood blockbuster for pure entertainment. "They are commodities to get a big return, the McDonalds of cinema."
Born in 1936 in the north of England, Loach, the son of an electrician, struggled for years on shoestring budgets because his unpopular brand of gritty social realism failed to fill cinema seats.

He has only begun to achieve recognition in Britain in the last few years, although he has long had a strong following in the rest of Europe. "Raining Stones" won the Jury Prize at the 1993 Cannes Film Festival and "Riff Raff" was nominated Best European Film of 1991.

"People in Britain are interested in these subjects but we don't have tradition of political cinema,". said Loach, a long-standing member of the main opposition Labour Party. "We tend to watch documentaries or read the papers instead."
